context: it means just what I choose it to mean
mainIdea: Humpty Dumpty says a word means just what he chooses it to mean, no more and no less.
simple: Humpty Dumpty said, in a rather scornful voice, that when he uses a word, it means exactly what he chooses it to mean. It does not mean more than that or less than that.

context: ‘slithy’ means ‘lithe and slimy.’ ‘Lithe’ is the same as ‘active.’
mainIdea: Humpty Dumpty explains the made-up word "slithy". He says it is like a portmanteau, with two meanings in one word.
simple: Humpty Dumpty said that "slithy" means "lithe and slimy". He said that "lithe" is the same as "active". He told Alice that it is like a portmanteau, because there are two meanings packed up into one word.

context: a ‘rath’ is a sort of green pig: but ‘mome’ I’m not certain about
mainIdea: Humpty Dumpty says what a rath is. He is not sure what "mome" means, but he gives his best idea.
simple: Humpty Dumpty said that a rath is a sort of green pig. He said he was not certain about "mome". He thought it was short for "from home", which would mean that they had lost their way.

context: To be able to see Nobody! And at that distance, too!
mainIdea: The King speaks as if Nobody were a person that Alice can see. He says his own eyes are not so good.
simple: The King said in an unhappy voice that he only wished he had such eyes: to be able to see Nobody, and from so far away! He said that it was as much as he could do to see real people by this light.

context: So of course Nobody walks slower than you
mainIdea: The Messenger says he passed Nobody on the road. The King takes "Nobody" to be a person who walks slower than the Messenger.
simple: The King said that was quite right, because the young lady had seen him too. So, he said, of course Nobody walks slower than the Messenger does.

context: First you take an upright stick,” said the Knight
mainIdea: The Knight describes his plan to stop hair falling off. You make your hair grow up a stick, because things never fall upwards.
simple: The Knight said that first you take a stick that stands straight up. Then you make your hair creep up it, like a fruit tree. He said the reason hair falls off is that it hangs down, and things never fall upwards. He said it is a plan of his own invention, and Alice may try it if she likes.

context: The only difficulty is with the feet: the head is high enough already
mainIdea: The Knight tells how he planned to get over a gate. He would put his head on the gate and stand on his head.
simple: The Knight said he would tell Alice how he came to think of it. He said he told himself that the only difficulty is with the feet, because the head is high enough already. So first he puts his head on the top of the gate. Then he stands on his head, and then the feet are high enough. Then he is over.

context: I don’t believe that pudding ever was cooked
mainIdea: The Knight says he does not think his new pudding was ever cooked, or will be. He still thinks it was a clever pudding to invent.
simple: The Knight said again that it was not the next day. He said that, in fact, and he held his head down and his voice got lower and lower, he did not believe that the pudding ever was cooked. He did not believe it ever would be cooked. And yet, he said, it was a very clever pudding to invent.

context: The bone wouldn’t remain, of course, if I took it
mainIdea: Alice answers the sum about taking a bone from a dog. She says the bone, the dog and she herself would not remain.
simple: Alice thought about it. She said that of course the bone would not remain if she took it. The dog would not remain either, because it would come to bite her. And she was sure that she would not remain!

context: we mostly have days and nights two or three at a time
mainIdea: The Red Queen says that in her country days and nights come together, and people join nights for warmth.
simple: The Red Queen said that Alice's way of having one day at a time is a poor, thin way of doing things. She said that here they mostly have days and nights two or three at a time. Sometimes in the winter they take as many as five nights together, for warmth.

context: it isn’t etiquette to cut anyone you’ve been introduced to
mainIdea: The Red Queen says it is not polite to cut someone you have met. The waiters take the leg of mutton away and bring a pudding.
simple: The Red Queen said very firmly, "Certainly not." She said that it is not proper behaviour to cut anyone you have been introduced to. She told the waiters to take the joint away. They carried it off and brought a large plum-pudding in its place.

context: The Red Queen made no resistance whatever
mainIdea: The Red Queen does not try to stop Alice shaking her. She grows smaller, fatter, softer and rounder.
simple: The Red Queen did not try to stop her at all. Only her face grew very small, and her eyes got large and green. And Alice went on shaking her, and she kept on growing shorter, fatter, softer and rounder, and ...

context: shook her backwards and forwards with all her might
mainIdea: Alice takes the Red Queen off the table and shakes her hard.
simple: Alice took the Queen off the table as she spoke. She shook her one way and then the other, as hard as she could.

context: whatever you say to them, they always purr
mainIdea: Alice thinks it is a bad habit of kittens that they always purr, whatever you say. This stops a conversation.
simple: Alice had once said that it is a very inconvenient habit of kittens that they always purr, whatever you say to them. She had said that if they would only purr for "yes" and mew for "no", or have any rule of that sort, one could keep up a conversation. But how can you talk with a person if they always say the same thing?

context: it must have been either me or the Red King
mainIdea: Alice asks Kitty to think who dreamed it all. She decides it was either herself or the Red King, and that each was part of the other's dream.
simple: Alice said to Kitty, "Let us think about who it was that dreamed it all." She said it is a serious question, and Kitty should not go on licking her paw, as if Dinah had not washed her that morning. She said it must have been either Alice or the Red King. He was part of her dream, but then she was part of his dream, too. She asked if it was the Red King, and said Kitty was his wife, so she ought to know. She asked Kitty to help to settle it, and said her paw could wait. But the annoying kitten only began on the other paw and pretended it had not heard the question.
